title: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) Differential Diagnosis
description: Differential diagnosis for acute kidney injury in adults, organized by prerenal, intrinsic renal, and postrenal etiologies as defined by the KDIGO 2012 AKI guideline.
source_description: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury. Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Acute Kidney Injury Work Group. Kidney Int Suppl 2012;2(1):1-138.

diagnoses.name: Prerenal Azotemia (Hypovolemia / Hypoperfusion)
key_features: History of volume loss (hemorrhage, vomiting, diarrhea, burns)
Hypotension or orthostatic changes
Concentrated urine with low fractional excretion of sodium (FENa <1%)
BUN-to-creatinine ratio >20:1
Rapid improvement with volume resuscitation
red_flags: Failure to respond to fluid challenge (suggests progression to ATN)
recommended_tests: Urinalysis with urine sodium and FENa
Fluid challenge with assessment of response

diagnoses.name: Sepsis-Associated AKI
key_features: Fever, hypotension, or signs of systemic infection
AKI in the context of documented or suspected infection
Often multifactorial (hemodynamic, inflammatory, nephrotoxic)
Most common cause of AKI in ICU patients

diagnoses.name: Acute Tubular Necrosis (Ischemic)
key_features: Follows prolonged hypotension, shock, or major surgery
Muddy brown granular casts on urine microscopy
FENa >2% (intrinsic renal injury)
Gradual creatinine rise over days
Oliguria followed by polyuric recovery phase
red_flags: Persistent oliguria or anuria beyond 2-3 weeks

diagnoses.name: Nephrotoxic Acute Tubular Necrosis
key_features: Temporal relationship to nephrotoxic drug exposure
Common culprits: aminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin B, cisplatin
Radiocontrast-induced AKI (typically 24-72 hours post-exposure)
Non-oliguric AKI more common with aminoglycosides
Muddy brown casts on urine microscopy
red_flags: Failure of creatinine to trend down after drug discontinuation
recommended_tests: Serum creatinine trend after drug withdrawal

diagnoses.name: Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN)
key_features: Drug-induced most common (antibiotics, NSAIDs, PPIs)
Classic triad: fever, rash, eosinophilia (present in <10% of cases)
White blood cell casts or eosinophiluria on urine microscopy
Non-oliguric AKI
Sterile pyuria
red_flags: Rapid creatinine rise with recent drug initiation
Failure to improve after offending drug withdrawal

diagnoses.name: Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN)
key_features: Rapid decline in renal function over days to weeks
Active urine sediment: dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts
Proteinuria (often nephritic range)
Causes: anti-GBM disease, ANCA vasculitis, lupus nephritis, IgA nephropathy

diagnoses.name: Obstructive Uropathy (Postrenal AKI)
key_features: Bilateral ureteral obstruction or bladder outlet obstruction
Common causes: BPH, pelvic malignancy, nephrolithiasis, neurogenic bladder
Hydronephrosis on renal ultrasound
May present with anuria or fluctuating urine output
Post-void residual >200 mL suggests bladder outlet obstruction
red_flags: Complete anuria (suggests bilateral or single-kidney obstruction)
Known pelvic malignancy with rising creatinine
recommended_tests: CT abdomen/pelvis without contrast if stone suspected

diagnoses.name: Cardiorenal Syndrome (Acute)
key_features: AKI in the setting of acute heart failure or cardiogenic shock
Venous congestion and reduced cardiac output both contribute
Elevated jugular venous pressure
Peripheral edema, pulmonary congestion
Creatinine rise with diuretic initiation or dose escalation
red_flags: Worsening renal function despite decongestive therapy
Need for inotropic support or mechanical circulatory assist

diagnoses.name: Hepatorenal Syndrome
key_features: AKI in setting of advanced cirrhosis and portal hypertension
Diagnosis of exclusion after prerenal and structural causes ruled out
No improvement with albumin volume expansion
Bland urine sediment, low urine sodium
Type 1 (rapid, doubling of creatinine in <2 weeks) vs Type 2 (gradual)
red_flags: Type 1 HRS with rapidly rising creatinine

diagnoses.name: Rhabdomyolysis-Induced AKI
key_features: Muscle injury from trauma, crush, prolonged immobilization, seizures, or statins
Markedly elevated creatine kinase (CK >5x upper limit of normal)
Dark (tea-colored) urine, positive dipstick for blood but few RBCs on microscopy
Myoglobin-induced tubular injury
Hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia disproportionate to renal failure

diagnoses.name: Thrombotic Microangiopathy (TMA)
key_features: AKI with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia
Includes TTP, HUS, and atypical HUS
Schistocytes on peripheral blood smear
Elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, indirect hyperbilirubinemia
May present with diarrhea (typical HUS) or neurologic symptoms (TTP)
red_flags: Pentad of TTP: thrombocytopenia, MAHA, AKI, neurologic symptoms, fever
recommended_tests: Stool culture and Shiga toxin assay

also_consider.name: Tumor Lysis Syndrome
also_consider.rationale: AKI with hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, and hyperphosphatemia after chemotherapy initiation; uric acid crystal deposition causes intratubular obstruction

also_consider.name: Atheroembolic Disease (Cholesterol Embolism)
also_consider.rationale: AKI after vascular procedure or anticoagulation; livedo reticularis, blue toe syndrome, and eosinophilia are diagnostic clues

also_consider.name: Renal Artery Thrombosis or Embolism
also_consider.rationale: Sudden AKI with flank pain and hematuria in patients with atrial fibrillation, endocarditis, or aortic disease; CT angiography is diagnostic

also_consider.name: Bilateral Renal Vein Thrombosis
also_consider.rationale: AKI with flank pain and nephrotic-range proteinuria; associated with nephrotic syndrome, malignancy, and hypercoagulable states

also_consider.name: Scleroderma Renal Crisis
also_consider.rationale: Acute hypertensive emergency with AKI in systemic sclerosis; requires urgent ACE inhibitor therapy

also_consider.name: Myeloma Cast Nephropathy
also_consider.rationale: AKI in older adults with unexplained anemia and bone pain; free light chains form obstructive casts in distal tubules

also_consider.name: Acute Cortical Necrosis
also_consider.rationale: Irreversible AKI after severe obstetric hemorrhage, abruptio placentae, or septic shock; cortical calcification on CT

also_consider.name: Acute Phosphate Nephropathy
also_consider.rationale: AKI following oral sodium phosphate bowel preparation; calcium phosphate crystal deposition in tubules

also_consider.name: IgA Vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein Purpura) Nephritis
also_consider.rationale: AKI with palpable purpura, arthralgia, and abdominal pain; renal involvement ranges from hematuria to RPGN

also_consider.name: Ethylene Glycol Poisoning
also_consider.rationale: AKI with high anion gap metabolic acidosis and osmolar gap; calcium oxalate crystals in urine are pathognomonic

also_consider.name: Abdominal Compartment Syndrome
also_consider.rationale: AKI due to elevated intra-abdominal pressure compressing renal vasculature; measure bladder pressure in critically ill with tense abdomen

also_consider.name: Malignant Hypertension with Renal Injury
also_consider.rationale: AKI with severely elevated blood pressure (>180/120), papilledema, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia; urgent blood pressure control needed

clinical_reasoning_prompt: This is an evidence-based reference set, not an exhaustive differential. AKI is frequently multifactorial -- consider overlapping prerenal, intrinsic, and postrenal contributions in the same patient. Always assess volume status, review medication list for nephrotoxins, obtain renal ultrasound to rule out obstruction, and examine urine sediment. In critically ill patients, multiple etiologies often coexist simultaneously. Consider the clinical context (community-acquired vs hospital-acquired, ICU vs ward) when prioritizing the differential.
